Your guess: Do students who study more score higher? Is each extra hour worth the same number of points? Are there any students who don’t fit the pattern?

Step 1: The basic scatterplot

TipReveal the scatterplot
Show the Python code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(data=scores, x="hours_studied", y="exam_score",
                color="#2a6f97", s=40, alpha=0.8, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Hours studied", ylabel="Exam score",
       title="More studying helps, but with diminishing returns")
plt.show()

Three things are visible at once:

  1. A clear positive relationship.
  2. It curves: the first few hours add a lot of points; hours 15–20 add very little.
  3. A small cluster of students who studied a lot but scored poorly.

That correlation coefficient, by the way, is r = 0.68. A single number can’t tell you about the curve or the cluster.

Step 2: Color by a third variable

What explains the low-scoring cluster? There’s one more column in the spreadsheet: whether the student attended the review session.

TipReveal the colored scatterplot
Show the Python code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(data=scores, x="hours_studied", y="exam_score", hue="attended_review",
                palette={"Yes": "#2a6f97", "No": "#d1495b"}, s=45, alpha=0.85, ax=ax)

# Smooth curve for students who attended, to show the bend
yes = scores[scores["attended_review"] == "Yes"].sort_values("hours_studied")
fit = np.polyfit(np.log1p(yes["hours_studied"]), yes["exam_score"], 1)
grid = np.linspace(0, 20, 200)
ax.plot(grid, np.polyval(fit, np.log1p(grid)), color="#2a6f97", lw=2, alpha=0.6)

ax.set(xlabel="Hours studied", ylabel="Exam score",
       title="The outliers all skipped the review session")
ax.legend(title="Attended review")
plt.show()

Every student in the odd cluster skipped the review session. Finding that from the table means checking 150 rows across three columns; in the chart it’s one glance at the red dots.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sim_data import study_scores

pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 500)
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", font_scale=1.05)
```

## Experiment: Does studying more pay off?

An instructor recorded how many hours each of 150 students studied for an exam and the score they earned.

::: {.raw-table}
```{python}
scores = study_scores()
scores[["student_id", "hours_studied", "exam_score"]]
```
:::

::: {.guess}
**Your guess:** Do students who study more score higher? Is each extra hour worth the same number of points? Are there any students who don't fit the pattern?
:::

## Step 1: The basic scatterplot

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reveal the scatterplot

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(data=scores, x="hours_studied", y="exam_score",
                color="#2a6f97", s=40, alpha=0.8, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Hours studied", ylabel="Exam score",
       title="More studying helps, but with diminishing returns")
plt.show()
```

[Three things are visible at once:]{.reveal-note}

1. A clear **positive** relationship.
2. It **curves**: the first few hours add a lot of points; hours 15–20 add very little.
3. A small **cluster of students** who studied a lot but scored poorly.

[That correlation coefficient, by the way, is r = `{python} f"{scores['hours_studied'].corr(scores['exam_score']):.2f}"`. A single number can't tell you about the curve or the cluster.]{.reveal-note}
:::

## Step 2: Color by a third variable

What explains the low-scoring cluster? There's one more column in the spreadsheet: whether the student attended the review session.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reveal the colored scatterplot

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(data=scores, x="hours_studied", y="exam_score", hue="attended_review",
                palette={"Yes": "#2a6f97", "No": "#d1495b"}, s=45, alpha=0.85, ax=ax)

# Smooth curve for students who attended, to show the bend
yes = scores[scores["attended_review"] == "Yes"].sort_values("hours_studied")
fit = np.polyfit(np.log1p(yes["hours_studied"]), yes["exam_score"], 1)
grid = np.linspace(0, 20, 200)
ax.plot(grid, np.polyval(fit, np.log1p(grid)), color="#2a6f97", lw=2, alpha=0.6)

ax.set(xlabel="Hours studied", ylabel="Exam score",
       title="The outliers all skipped the review session")
ax.legend(title="Attended review")
plt.show()
```

[Every student in the odd cluster skipped the review session. Finding that from the table means checking 150 rows across three columns; in the chart it's one glance at the red dots.]{.reveal-note}
:::
